title: Schema enforcement shim and compatibility test harness for constrained decoding with streaming
creator: Priya Desai
description: Objective: Build a focused test harness and small middleware shim that validates end-to-end behavior for 'JSON mode' enforcement across streaming responses and tool/function-calling flows, with an emphasis on decoder compatibility modes (strict schema enforcement, graceful fallback, and partial-output recovery).
background: We have multiple tickets validating structured outputs, but gaps remain around streaming scenarios and tool-calling compatibility. Existing e2e checks assume non-streaming final payloads; in production we see two classes of failure: 1) partial tokens emitted during streaming break downstream JSON parsers, and 2) model variant fallbacks produce subtly different shaped outputs that violate strict schema validators. This ticket creates an isolated harness + shim that exercises constrained-decoding kernels and compatibility layers to assert expected behavior and surface regressions before runtime rollouts.
acceptance_criteria: A deterministic test harness that can run locally and in CI to simulate streaming tokens with controlled delays and token fragmentation
A lightweight enforcement shim (language-agnostic pseudocode reference + Go/TS examples) that intercepts streaming chunks and performs incremental schema validation without blocking throughput
Automated scenarios that validate tool/function-calling handshake semantics when the model returns streaming structured outputs (including function-embedding boundaries and nested tool call args)
Regression tests for at least three compatibility modes: strict, tolerant-with-warnings, and best-effort-repair (with an audit trail)
CI gates that fail on newly introduced strict-mode regressions and add warnings for tolerant-mode diffs
Linked docs and a demo that show how to use the harness to reproduce a production incident within 10 minutes
design_notes: Trade-offs considered: 1) full AST streaming validator vs incremental predicate checking — we chose incremental predicate checking to avoid heavyweight parsing on every chunk. 2) Blocking validation while rebuffering improves correctness but hurts latency; our shim provides configurable SLO-aware timeouts and emits a policy decision (reject | repair | allow-with-warning). 3) Repair strategies are heuristic: we prefer deterministic normalization rules (e.g., closing braces, canonicalizing number formats) and record all repairs in the audit log for later review.
implementation_plan: 1) Create simulator that feeds token chunks with configurable entropy (broken tokens, delayed tokens, truncated structures). 2) Implement shim in Go (runtime) and a reference TS helper for SDKs. 3) Write CI jobs that run the harness against current constrained-decoding kernels and the compatibility fallback logic. 4) Add dashboards to track failures and the frequency of repair-mode activations. 5) Run a pilot on `canary/runtime-1.20` with synthetic traffic and one internal customer workload.
test_matrix: Streaming fragmentation: single-field fragmentation, nested-object fragmentation, array-chunking
Tool-calling: function name mismatch mid-stream, arguments split across chunks, multiple nested tool calls
Compatibility variants: full-precision model output, quantized variant outputs, trimmed-token variant
Load profiles: low-latency single request, sustained high-throughput batching, slow-client backpressure
risks_mitigation: Risk: Repair heuristics may mask upstream model regressions. Mitigation: all repairs are logged and surfaced to quality dashboards; strict-mode CI will fail on any repair that changes required schema fields. Risk: shim adds latency under heavy backpressure. Mitigation: SLO-aware timeouts and per-request policy that can fall back to 'allow-with-warning' under overload.
